To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
antenatal exposures to indoor air pollution, tobacco smoke, and volatile organic compound exposures are associated with severe lower respiratory tract infections and wheeze in African infants.

antenatal exposure to indoor air pollutants or maternal smoking is the most significant risk factor for lower respiratory tract illness or wheezing during infancy, and that exposure to toluene is a novel risk factor for severe lower respiratory tract illness.

Antenatal maternal smoking and exposure to particulate matter were the predominant risk exposures for lower respiratory tract infections and wheeze in African infants, with toluene exposure a novel risk factor for severe lower respiratory tract infections.

the effects of early-life exposure to indoor pollutants on respiratory health and the mechanisms underlying these effects.
the impact of early life exposures on the development of asthma and other respiratory conditions.
the impact of environmental exposures on the respiratory health of children in low- and middle-income countries.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that exposure to environmental tobacco smoke (passive smoking) in the womb is associated with an increase in lower respiratory tract illness in infants, and that exposure to volatile organic compounds (such as toluene) in the womb can lead to severe respiratory illness requiring hospitalisation.
we have shown that early life exposure to IAP and ECTS are risk factors for lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI), which are associated with wheezing in infants.

we have shown that exposure to environmental tobacco smoke (both maternal smoking and household member smoking) and to indoor air pollution (particulate pollution, nitrogen dioxide, toluene, benzene, and carbon monoxide) is associated with lower respiratory illness or wheezing, and that the antenatal period is the most critical time of life for these exposures.
The main takeaway from our work is that

exposure to indoor air pollutants and environmental tobacco smoke during the antenatal period has a significant impact on the development of respiratory illnesses in children, and this effect is independent of the postnatal period.
antenatal exposures are the predominant risk factors for LRTI and wheezing illness in African infants.

exposure to environmental tobacco smoke and to indoor air pollution during pregnancy, and to indoor air pollutants during infancy, is a risk factor for lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) and wheezing.
